strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely new problem framing — multi-level non-IID knowledge sharing in FL — and a method (FeMAM) that unifies global, clustered, and personalized FL under one additive composition, which is a natural and well-motivated extension of prior two-level additive models [18, 34].

Experiments are fairly extensive: two datasets, multiple non-IID partitions (cluster-wise, Dirichlet client-wise, synthetic multi-level, IID), four random seeds, ablations over level components, runtime/communication analysis, and structure-discovery visualizations (Fig. 4, A.1) that show FeMAM recovers the planted multi-level structure — evidence that goes beyond raw accuracy numbers.
The 'No Free Lunch' appendix honestly discusses the added storage, inference, and communication costs, which is a welcome treatment of limitations rather than overselling.
The adaptive mechanisms (progressive level adding, pruning by validation-loss improvement, greedy per-client model selection) are sensible and ablation Table 2 shows each level contributes.
Convergence analysis is provided for both the EM (clustering) objective and the FL objective, with proofs in the appendix.
weaknesses: Practicality and generality concerns: the method relies on each client having a local validation set for pruning (Eq. 9) and convergence monitoring, which is a strong and non-standard assumption in cross-device FL that is not ablated; the number of clusters per middle level is fixed to 5 regardless of the true structure, and L=5 with a fixed 400-round first level suggests substantial engineering sensitivity that is not analyzed.

Limited empirical scope for an ICML main-track claim of 'surpassing methods by a large margin': only Tiny ImageNet and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-9 and 50 clients; no larger datasets, no larger/client-scaled settings, and no comparison against several recent clustered/personalized FL baselines (e.g., IFCA is cited but not compared).

The contribution over the closest prior work [34] (clustered additive modeling with a global model plus one cluster level) is incremental — essentially repeating the cluster level across multiple levels — and the paper does not sharply delineate what new technical difficulty the multi-level case introduces beyond notation.

Theoretical results are weak in practice: Theorem 2 assumes convex local losses (contradicting the deep-network experiments), and the derived learning-rate conditions depend on unknown quantities (distances between local and cluster models, gradient variances), so the analysis offers limited actionable insight; the proof structure largely follows [24].

Writing and presentation issues undermine polish: the abstract ends mid-sentence ('Our code is available at' with a blank link), several typos and grammatical errors ('conduc-t', Eq. 5 'concrete Eq. (3)'), and an inconsistency between Section 5.1 (validation = half of testing set) and Appendix C.1 (validation split from training set) that makes exact evaluation protocol ambiguous.

Baseline fairness is questionable: FedSEM's cluster count is fixed at 5 across all settings including cluster-wise partitions with different true cluster counts, and it is unclear whether baselines received comparable per-setting tuning; the multi-level data partitions are synthetic constructions whose real-world prevalence is asserted but not demonstrated.

Cost accounting, while honest, reveals a substantial practical burden: training proceeds level-by-level (400 rounds for level 1 plus 50+ per level), and wall-clock time, though plotted, is not contextualized against the accuracy gains per unit cost for a clear efficiency claim.

strengths: The paper identifies an underexplored problem setting: fine-grained, multi-level knowledge-sharing structure across federated clients, which is a natural generalization beyond global/clustered/personalized FL.

The proposed FeMAM method is concretely specified (Algorithms 1 and 2), combining FedAvg at level 1, K-means-style clustering (à la FeSEM) at intermediate levels, and local fine-tuning at the final level, with a practical progressive level-adding scheme and validation-based model pruning.

Experiments are reasonably extensive for the setting: two datasets (CIFAR-100, Tiny ImageNet), three families of non-IID partitions plus IID, multiple baselines from global, clustered, and personalized FL, accuracy and Macro-F1, with 4 independent runs and error bars.

The analysis of the learned multi-level structures (Fig. 4, Fig. A.1, Fig. C.1–C.2) and the ablation removing levels (Table 2) give useful insight into what the method actually learns, and the appendix honestly discusses the 'no free lunch' costs in storage, communication, and inference.
Convergence analysis is provided for both the clustering (EM) objective and the FL objective, with proofs in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the method is essentially a sequential composition of existing components (FedAvg, FeSEM/IFCA-style clustered FL from [13], additive residual modeling from [18, 34, 35], and local fine-tuning). The main new ingredient is stacking these into L levels with validation-based pruning, which feels incremental rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The evaluation is confined to synthetic, self-defined multi-level partitions on two image classification benchmarks with a small model (ResNet-9) and 50 clients. There is no evidence on realistic federated workloads (e.g., natural partition benchmarks, NLP, larger models, cross-silo/cross-device heterogeneity), so the practical significance of the 'multi-level non-IID' setting remains unestablished.

The method has practical requirements that weaken its applicability: each client must maintain a held-out validation set (half the test-set size) used for checkpoint selection, level-convergence detection, and pruning decisions; and training is strictly sequential across levels (400 rounds for level 1 alone), which the convergence analysis does not meaningfully account for.

The theoretical results are weak relative to the claims. The convergence guarantees inherit restrictive assumptions from [24], notably convexity of the local loss, which is unrealistic for the deep networks used in the experiments, and the learning-rate conditions in Theorem 2 depend on unknown quantities (e.g., gradient norms, distance to cluster centroids) that cannot be verified in practice. No explicit convergence rates are derived.

Cluster counts at intermediate levels are fixed at K=5 regardless of the ground-truth structure (e.g., 9, 15, or 22 clusters), and the paper acknowledges FeMAM cannot recover the full multi-level structure; thus the 'structure discovery' claim is only partially supported.

Baseline coverage is incomplete: closely related clustered-FL methods discussed in Related Works (e.g., IFCA [12], hierarchical clustering [23]) are cited but not compared, and comparisons rely mainly on FeSEM variants from the same research group.

Presentation issues undermine polish: the abstract and code link are truncated/broken, there are multiple typos and informal statements (e.g., 'Baselines only perform well on the desired non-IID'), and some notation (mapping functions C_l, c_l, the pruning threshold in Eq. 9) requires effort to parse.

The pruning rule with ε=0 makes hard binary decisions from noisy validation estimates; no sensitivity analysis of ε or of the convergence-detection heuristic (variance over last 50 rounds) is provided, raising reproducibility and robustness concerns.

Fairness of comparison is unclear: FeMAM effectively trains a sequence of models with access to per-client validation data for model selection and pruning, while baselines do not exploit these additional signals in the same way; the wall-clock and communication analysis (Fig. 5) partially addresses this but does not fully neutralize the advantage.

strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes an interesting and underexplored problem: non-IID structure in federated learning that spans multiple granularity levels (global, cluster, and client), and proposes a natural additive-modeling formulation in which each client's predictor is the sum of outputs from models at several levels.

The proposed FeMAM algorithm is well-motivated and practical: progressive level adding, level-wise alternating optimization with frozen lower levels, and validation-based model pruning make the potentially complex joint objective tractable, and the communication cost analysis (Appendix A, Fig. 5) is a welcome treatment of overhead.

The experiments are reasonably comprehensive: two datasets (CIFAR-100, Tiny ImageNet), four non-IID regimes including a specifically constructed multi-level partition, several strong baselines spanning global/clustered/personalized FL (FedAvg, FedProx, pFedMe, FedRep, Ditto, FeSEM), with error bars over 4 runs.

The structure-discovery analysis (Fig. 4, Appendix A/C) is convincing evidence that the method recovers the planted relation structure via pruning, and the ablation in Table 2 isolates the contribution of each level.
A convergence analysis is provided, with assumptions stated and proofs in the appendix, building on the EM-based clustered-FL analysis of Ma et al. [24].
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to prior work: the method is essentially a multi-level extension of clustered additive modeling (FeSEM [34], federated residual learning [18], [35]), combining FedAvg (level 1), K-means-based clustered FL (levels 2..L-1), and local fine-tuning (level L). The claim of being 'the first to propose a Multi-level Non-IID setting' overstates novelty given existing hierarchical clustering FL (e.g., [23]) and hierarchical FL literature.

A theory-practice gap weakens the convergence results: Theorem 2 assumes convex, Lipschitz-smooth losses, but all experiments use ResNet-9, which violates these assumptions. Moreover, the assumed learning-rate bounds depend on quantities (B, U, gradient norms) that are not estimable in practice, so the theory offers limited practical guidance. The analysis is a fairly direct level-wise adaptation of [24].

Fairness of comparison concerns: FeMAM uses 5 levels with 5 clusters each (25+ models), substantially more total model capacity than most baselines; the fixed L=5 and K=5 align conveniently with the synthetic multi-level ground truths (e.g., 3,6,11), and ground-truth structures are known when designing the experiments. Sensitivity to misspecified L and K is not systematically studied.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only two image classification benchmarks with CNNs, no language/tabular tasks, no cross-silo or cross-device scale variation, and no comparison with several relevant methods (e.g., IFCA empirically, FedProto, hierarchical FL baselines).

The method requires clients to hold a local validation set (pruning with epsilon=0 and level-adding decisions depend on it), which is a nontrivial assumption in FL; how the validation split affects low-data clients and robustness of the pruning criterion is not analyzed. Pruning with epsilon=0 also risks validation overfitting.

Communication/computation costs are non-negligible: the first level requires ~400 rounds before adding new levels, and total wall-clock exceeds FedAvg (Fig. 5a); the paper's framing of this as 'acceptable' would benefit from a more careful accounting and from convergence-time comparisons at matched accuracy.

Presentation has notable rough edges: the code link in the abstract is a placeholder; Eq. (5) writes a 'min' over cluster assignment inside the objective while (D.3) uses argmin, creating inconsistency; several grammatical errors ('Eq. (5) concrete Eq. (3)', 'at this two steps', 'when the it converges'); Theorem 1's statement is compressed and hard to parse on first reading.

strengths: The multi-level non-IID framing is well-motivated and clearly distinguishes FeMAM from fixed two-level (global+cluster or global+client) designs in clustered and personalized FL.

The grow-and-prune mechanism is a sensible way to avoid pre-specifying hierarchy depth, and the client-specific pruning (Eq. 7) gives an interpretable 'on-demand personalization depth'; the structure visualizations (Fig. 5, Fig. A.1) showing recovered cluster boundaries vs. ground truth are a nice empirical contribution.

Experiments are comparatively broad: two image benchmarks with three constructed non-IID partitions, ablations on L and K, runtime/communication cost analyses, and a foundation-model setting (Qwen3-4B with LoRA over 71 FLAN tasks) that is more contemporary than typical PFL evaluations.
The paper includes an honest limitations section (limited exploration of level-wise components, small scale of the foundation-model evaluation), which is appropriately candid rather than defensive.
Cost analysis is addressed concretely: per-round communication matches single-model FL, stored-model counts (Table 4) are reported, and wall-clock comparison (Fig. 7a) shows only moderate overhead.
weaknesses: A key methodological ambiguity is unaddressed: additive composition sums the outputs of independently trained neural networks (e.g., logits of a FedAvg model plus logits of K-means-clustered models plus a locally fine-tuned model). How this composition behaves when Level-1 is trained as a full standalone predictor (Eq. 1 loss) and later levels must learn corrections on top of already-saturated predictions is never analyzed or discussed; the paper would benefit from justification or ablation of the composition mechanism itself.

The theoretical contribution is weak relative to its billing. The monotone descent claim (D.14/D.17) leans on Assumption D.5 ('boosting edge / residual alignment'), which essentially assumes the level-l predictor is sufficiently aligned with the residual — i.e., the central descent property is assumed rather than proven, and γ_l is never measured empirically. The remaining lemmas are standard local-SGD/smoothness arguments the authors themselves label 'routine'. The pruning argument also guarantees per-client non-increase on client data, which is conflated with non-increase of the aggregate objective R_l after assignments change.

The mechanism behind FeMAM's gains is not fully disentangled: the hierarchy includes a fully local fine-tuning level (K5 = 50), which is also the strongest component under client-wise heterogeneity; an ablation isolating the contribution of intermediate cluster levels versus simply global+local (e.g., FedPer/Ditto-style) composition is not clearly presented, making it hard to attribute the improvement to the multi-level structure rather than the personal level.

Baseline comparability concerns: FeMAM uses a 5-level sequential schedule (400 + 4×50 rounds) with a large personalization level, and clustered baselines (FeSEM) show implausibly poor results on client-wise non-IID (22.3% on Tiny ImageNet), raising tuning questions; assignment criteria (K-means on parameters, Eq. C.3) are heuristic and differ from the loss-based routing the theory's slack analysis describes as the favorable case.

Reproducibility is undercut: the 'Code:' field in the abstract is empty, and no code or anonymized repository is referenced anywhere, despite the method having many implementation-sensitive choices (assignment criteria, pruning threshold, convergence-variance rule, composition details).

Writing has notable sloppiness for a main-track submission (e.g., 'Numerica:', 'FeMAM's can effectively adapt', 'Table 3 study'), and the novelty is moderate — it is a fairly direct extension of two-level additive clustered modeling (FedCAM, Agarwal et al.) to multiple levels with boosting-style scheduling, so the framing of a 'new requirement' for FL algorithms somewhat overstates the conceptual jump.

strengths: The multi-level non-IID perspective is clearly motivated, and FeMAM provides a coherent framework that generalizes two-level additive/clustered FL (e.g., FedCAM, Agarwal et al. 2020) to multiple granularities with grow-and-prune level-wise training.

The empirical evaluation is broad relative to typical FL papers: two image benchmarks under three non-IID partition types plus a foundation-model (Qwen3-4B + LoRA) task-partitioned setting, with ablations on L and K, cost/communication analysis, and visualization of learned structures (Fig. 5, Fig. A.1).
The paper is generally well organized, includes an honest limitations section acknowledging limited level-wise component exploration and small-scale evaluation, and declares no conflicts of interest.
Cost claims are at least partially supported: per-round communication and training only involve the current level, and pruning reduces stored models in practice (Table 4).
weaknesses: Limited originality: the contribution is largely a composition of known ingredients—additive residual composition (Agarwal et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2023), boosting-style sequential training (Friedman, 2001), cluster assignments (IFCA/FeSEM), and per-client validation pruning. Extending a fixed two-level additive design to L levels is an incremental generalization rather than a new understanding.

The convergence analysis is largely circular or trivial. Assumption D.5 ('boosting edge') assumes exactly the property that new-level predictions align with the residual gradient (with constant γ_l), which is the central thing one would want to establish; the monotone descent across levels (D.14) follows directly from the pruning rule by construction. The remaining lemmas are routine local-SGD/aggregation bounds under restrictive assumptions (D.1–D.4), so the theory adds little genuine insight.

Important practical details that affect feasibility and fairness are not adequately addressed or ablated: client-side structure pruning (Eq. 7) and loss-based assignment (Eq. 5) require clients to hold validation data, which is not standard in FL and is not discussed in terms of privacy or data-split realism; clients must store up to L full models for inference, and the claim that 'inference latency can be close to that of a single model' via parallel evaluation is asserted without measurement, particularly unrealistic on resource-constrained edge devices that motivate the work.

Missing strong/simple baselines weaken the empirical claims: there is no comparison against a straightforward two-level stack (e.g., FedAvg + cluster models + local fine-tuning without the multi-level machinery), nor against simply ensembling FedAvg with Local. Some baseline results appear misconfigured or implausible (e.g., FeSEM at 22–25% accuracy on Client-wise Dirichlet non-IID, well below Local), casting doubt on tuning fairness. FeMAM also uses a different training schedule (400 + 50×4 rounds) and far more total model capacity than baselines, complicating comparisons.

The claim that Dirichlet client-wise partition 'can exhibit implicit multi-level structure' is asserted but not substantiated with evidence connecting learned structures to any actual ground truth; the structural analysis on Cluster-wise/Multi-level settings uses synthetic label-based partitions whose cluster counts (e.g., 3/6/11, 9/15/22) already exceed K=5, so the learned hierarchies only partially match the ground truth by the authors' own admission.

Reproducibility concerns: the code link in the abstract is empty ('Code:'), and several details needed to reproduce the method (validation-set construction per client, convergence threshold, assignment criterion per level in the main experiments, hyperparameters for baselines like PM-MoE) are incomplete or deferred. Minor presentation issues (e.g., 'Numerica:', inconsistent CIFAR naming) suggest a rushed manuscript.

Significance is moderate: the simulated experiments use a small model (ResNet-9) and 50 clients, and the foundation-model experiment uses short-sequence FLAN tasks with ~300 training samples per client and rank-4 LoRA over 100 rounds—far from the 'large-scale, contemporary' framing in the introduction.

strengths: The multi-level non-IID framing is well-motivated and clearly distinguishes FeMAM from two-granularity clustered FL and global-local PFL methods, which capture at most one intermediate sharing level.

The grow-and-prune design is practically appealing: level-wise sequential training keeps per-round communication and training cost comparable to single-model FL, and client-side validation-based pruning yields on-demand personalization depth (supported by Table 4 and Fig. 5).

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad: controlled single-level (cluster-wise), client-wise, and explicitly multi-level non-IID partitions on two image benchmarks, an ablation over both L and K, runtime/communication-cost analysis (Fig. 7), and a contemporary foundation-model experiment with LoRA on Qwen3-4B over 71 heterogeneous FLAN/LoraHub tasks.

FeMAM achieves the best reported accuracy/Macro-F1 in nearly all simulated conditions (Table 1) and the best loss and ROUGE-1 in the foundation-model setting (Table 5), including against strong recent baselines (PM-MoE, pFedMoE, FedCAM).

The learned-structure visualizations (Fig. 5, Fig. A.1) provide a useful interpretability story: pruning behavior adapts sensibly to the ground-truth heterogeneity (sparse under IID/cluster-wise, deep under multi-level), and the K-sensitivity ablation (Table 3) supports the claim that clustering acts as structure sampling.

The paper is honest about limitations: it acknowledges that only one instantiation of level-wise components was tested, and that the foundation-model evaluation is small in scale relative to realistic deployments.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is shallow relative to its framing. Assumption D.5 (the 'boosting edge') simply assumes that the new level's predictor is aligned with the residual (inner product lower bound), which is precisely the property a convergence analysis of boosting-style methods should establish. The resulting descent (Eq. D.17–D.18) is then a standard conditional guarantee rather than a genuine convergence result for the proposed algorithm. The paper candidly calls this 'convergence intuition', but the contribution bullet claiming 'a convergence analysis for the proposed multi-level framework' overstates it.

There is a potential train/validation mismatch in the monotone-descent argument: pruning (Eq. 7) is based on validation error, yet the non-increase R_l <= R_{l-1} (D.14) is stated for the training objective. The proof does not reconcile this gap, so the monotone descent claim does not strictly follow from the actual algorithm.

Assumption D.4 abstracts the assignment update with a slack epsilon_l but does not bound epsilon_l for the K-means assignment actually used in experiments; the discussion defers to prior work (Ma et al., 2022) rather than deriving the constant, leaving the practical relevance of the bound unclear.

Originality is moderate: the framework is a natural extension of two-level additive/clustered modeling (Agarwal et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2023) and boosting-style sequential model addition to multiple levels, combined with validation-based pruning; each ingredient is individually well-established.

Additive composition of full-network logits across separately trained ResNets is architecturally unusual, and the paper provides limited analysis of why stacked additive refinement works for deep models beyond the residual-learning analogy; the shared-extractor variant that would make this more natural is mentioned but not evaluated.

Reproducibility concerns: the code link on page 1 is empty ('Code:' with no repository), and several hyperparameters important for the method (e.g., the lambda in the instantiated objective C.3, convergence criterion details) are only partially specified. The 'Code' omission is a notable gap for an empirical paper.

Some reported margins are small relative to the strongest baselines (e.g., CIFAR-100 cluster-wise accuracy 53.72 vs. 53.29 for PM-MoE, Macro-F1 48.33 vs. 47.89 for FedCAM), and while results are averaged over 4 runs, no statistical significance testing is provided.

Writing has minor defects ('Numerica:' on page 8, Table 3 caption placement, an empty code field), and the fairness of comparisons could be stated more carefully: FeMAM uses a 400+50x4 round schedule and a validation set for both checkpoint selection and pruning decisions, while baselines use the validation set only for checkpoint selection; the extra per-client validation data usage for pruning should be discussed as part of the method's data assumptions.

The foundation-model experiment, while a strength in scope, is small (300 training samples per task, 100 rounds, ROUGE-1 only), so its evidence for the central multi-level claim is correspondingly limited — acknowledged by the authors but it weakens the generality claim.
